clinicalPearls: Progressive dysphagia to both solids AND liquids from the outset is the classic clue distinguishing achalasia from a mechanical stricture or malignancy, where solid-food dysphagia usually predominates and progresses later to liquids.
Regurgitation of undigested food (especially at night, with risk of aspiration) and slow, gradual weight loss are common accompanying features.
Retrosternal chest pain/discomfort with meals occurs in a subset of patients, more often early in the disease course.
Patients often learn compensatory maneuvers — eating slowly, holding arms overhead, or performing repeated swallows/Valsalva — to help push food through the non-relaxing lower esophageal sphincter.
Barium esophagram classically shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction.
Manometry is the gold standard: it shows absent/incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation together with loss of normal peristalsis in the esophageal body.
New-onset 'achalasia-like' symptoms in an older adult, especially with rapid weight loss, should prompt evaluation for pseudoachalasia from a malignancy at the gastroesophageal junction.
Chagas disease should be considered in patients from or with travel history to endemic areas of Latin America presenting with an achalasia-like picture.
harrison.pathophysiology: Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophagus, leading to loss of coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax appropriately with swallowing. The cause is usually idiopathic, though an autoimmune or postviral inflammatory process targeting these neurons is suspected in many cases. Similar clinical pictures can arise secondarily from infiltrative or destructive processes affecting the myenteric plexus, such as Chagas disease or tumor invasion at the gastroesophageal junction (pseudoachalasia).
additionalDifferentials: Distal esophageal spasm and other esophageal motility disorders
Gastroesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture
Esophageal or gastric cardia malignancy causing pseudoachalasia
infectionMimics: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causing destruction of myenteric plexus with achalasia-like esophageal dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Barium esophagram — shows esophageal dilation with distal 'bird's beak' tapering and poor emptying
High-resolution esophageal manometry — confirms diagnosis via absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation, and subtypes achalasia (I–III)
Upper endoscopy — mandatory to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause (pseudoachalasia) at or near the gastroesophageal junction
Endoscopic ultrasound or CT chest/abdomen — used selectively when pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration is suspected
Serology for Trypanosoma cruzi — considered in patients from endemic regions to exclude Chagas disease
Timed barium swallow — assesses esophageal emptying and is useful for monitoring treatment response
Chest imaging — may incidentally reveal a dilated, air/fluid-filled esophagus or absent gastric air bubble
redFlags: Rapid symptom onset or significant weight loss in an older patient, raising concern for pseudoachalasia due to malignancy
Recurrent aspiration pneumonia from nocturnal regurgitation
Severe odynophagia or evidence of esophageal perforation
Marked, progressive esophageal dilation (megaesophagus) with risk of retained food and aspiration
New or worsening symptoms despite treatment, warranting re-evaluation for an underlying malignant cause
pitfalls: Attributing dysphagia to reflux disease and delaying manometry, since achalasia can be misdiagnosed as GERD for years
Failing to perform endoscopy to exclude a malignant or infiltrative cause before treating for idiopathic achalasia
Overlooking Chagas disease in patients with relevant epidemiologic exposure
Assuming a normal-caliber esophagus on barium study excludes achalasia; early disease may show minimal dilation despite abnormal manometry
harrison.prognosis: With appropriate treatment (pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy), most patients achieve durable symptomatic improvement, though the underlying esophageal aperistalsis is not reversed and long-term surveillance is often needed. Untreated or longstanding disease carries risk of progressive esophageal dilation, aspiration, malnutrition, and a modestly increased long-term risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Esophageal Motility Disorders (Dysphagia/Diseases of the Esophagus section)
